stem: Write the structural formula and IUPAC names of all possible isomers of the compound with molecular formula C₃H₈O. Write 'two' uses of phenol.
solution:
The molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_8O}\) satisfies \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}O}\), so every isomer is saturated and open chain and carries one oxygen. Three such structures are possible, two alcohols and one ether.

**1. Propan-1-ol** (n-propyl alcohol), a primary alcohol :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-OH}\)

**2. Propan-2-ol** (isopropyl alcohol), a secondary alcohol :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3}\)

**3. Methoxyethane** (ethyl methyl ether) :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-O-CH_2-CH_3}\)

Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol differ only in the position of the hydroxyl group, so they are position isomers of each other. Methoxyethane carries an ethereal oxygen in place of the hydroxyl group, so it is a functional isomer of both alcohols.

**Two uses of phenol :**

1. Phenol is used as an antiseptic and disinfectant; the dilute aqueous solution known as carbolic lotion is used to disinfect floors, drains and surgical instruments.

2. Phenol is the starting material for the manufacture of phenol-formaldehyde resins such as bakelite, and of medicines such as aspirin and salol.

Each of the three structures accounts for three carbons, eight hydrogens and one oxygen, so the set is complete for this formula.

stem: Write structural formula of the alcohol that results when acetaldehyde is reacted with \(\text{CH}_{3}\text{MgBr}\) in the presence of dry ether and the product is hydrolysed.
solution:
A Grignard reagent adds across the carbonyl group of an aldehyde. The carbon joined to magnesium carries a partial negative charge and attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, while \(\mathrm{MgBr}\) goes to the oxygen. Dry ether is the solvent because the reagent is destroyed by even traces of moisture.

**Step 1 : addition.**

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO} + \mathrm{CH_3MgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OMgBr)-CH_3}\)

(Acetaldehyde) + (Methyl magnesium bromide) \(\longrightarrow\) (Addition product)

**Step 2 : hydrolysis.** Dilute acid replaces \(\mathrm{OMgBr}\) by the hydroxyl group.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OMgBr)-CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3} + \mathrm{Mg(OH)Br}\)

The structural formula of the alcohol formed is

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3}\)

which is propan-2-ol, isopropyl alcohol. The carbinol carbon carries two alkyl groups and one hydrogen, so the product is a secondary alcohol, which is what any aldehyde other than formaldehyde must give with a Grignard reagent.

stem: Write the balanced chemical equation for the following: \(\text{i}\). Action of sodium metal on ethanol.
solution:
The hydrogen of the hydroxyl group of ethanol is weakly acidic, so an active metal such as sodium displaces it as hydrogen gas and sodium ethoxide is left behind. The brisk effervescence of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is the standard test for an alcoholic \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group.

\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{H_2}\uparrow\)

(Ethanol) + (Sodium) \(\longrightarrow\) (Sodium ethoxide) + (Hydrogen)

The equation is balanced : four carbons, twelve hydrogens, two oxygens and two sodium atoms appear on each side.

stem: Identify 'A', 'B' and 'C' in the following chain reaction and rewrite the chemical reactions:
solution:
The reagents of the chain are read from the scheme printed with the question : ethanol is treated with red phosphorus and bromine, the product with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KCN}\), and that product with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) in ether.

**Step 1 : ethanol to the alkyl bromide.** Red phosphorus with bromine generates phosphorus tribromide in the reaction mixture, and \(\mathrm{PBr_3}\) replaces the hydroxyl group of the alcohol by bromine.

\(3\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH} + \mathrm{PBr_3} \longrightarrow 3\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-Br} + \mathrm{H_3PO_3}\)

**A is bromoethane (ethyl bromide),** \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br}\).

**Step 2 : nucleophilic substitution by cyanide.** Potassium cyanide is ionic, and in alcoholic medium the cyanide ion attacks through its carbon atom, so the alkyl cyanide is the product.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-Br} + \mathrm{KCN} \xrightarrow{\text{alc.}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C \equiv N} + \mathrm{KBr}\)

**B is propanenitrile (ethyl cyanide),** \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN}\).

**Step 3 : reduction of the nitrile.** Lithium aluminium hydride in ether delivers four hydrogen atoms across the carbon-nitrogen triple bond and a primary amine is obtained.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C \equiv N} \xrightarrow[\text{ether}]{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2}\)

**C is propan-1-amine (n-propylamine),** \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\).

The carbon count is consistent throughout : ethanol has two carbons, A has two, the cyanide group adds one so B has three, and the amine C also has three.

stem: Convert the following: \(\text{i}\). Acetaldehyde to isopropyl alcohol.
solution:
Isopropyl alcohol is propan-2-ol and has three carbon atoms, while acetaldehyde has two. One carbon must therefore be added, and a Grignard reagent does this and installs the hydroxyl group in the same operation.

**Step 1 : addition of methyl magnesium bromide.** The nucleophilic methyl carbon of the reagent attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde and \(\mathrm{MgBr}\) goes to the oxygen. Dry ether is used as the solvent.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO} + \mathrm{CH_3MgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OMgBr)-CH_3}\)

**Step 2 : hydrolysis.** Dilute acid replaces \(\mathrm{OMgBr}\) by \(\mathrm{OH}\).

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OMgBr)-CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3}\)

(Acetaldehyde) \(\longrightarrow\) (Propan-2-ol, isopropyl alcohol)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3}\) has three carbons and a hydroxyl group on the middle one, so it is the required isopropyl alcohol, and being secondary it is what an aldehyde must give with a Grignard reagent.

stem: Write the structural formula and \(\text{IUPAC}\) name of the alcohol having molecular formula \(\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}\) which does not undergo oxidation under normal condition.
solution:
An alcohol is oxidised at the carbon that carries the hydroxyl group, and that carbon must hold at least one hydrogen for the oxidation to take place. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen there, so it resists oxidation under ordinary conditions.

Of the alcohols of molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\), only one is tertiary.

**Structural formula :**

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH}\), that is \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)(OH)-CH_3}\)

**IUPAC name : 2-methylpropan-2-ol** (tert-butyl alcohol).

The carbinol carbon here is joined to three methyl groups and to the hydroxyl group, and has no hydrogen of its own, so an oxidising agent finds no \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond at that carbon to break and no carbonyl compound can be formed.

The three other isomeric alcohols do carry such a hydrogen and are oxidised readily : butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are primary and give an aldehyde and then an acid, and butan-2-ol is secondary and gives a ketone.

stem: Explain the mechanism of esterification. Explain the reaction involved in dehydration of \(1^{\circ}\), \(2^{\circ}\) and \(3^{\circ}\) alcohols.
solution:
**Part 1 : mechanism of esterification.**

A carboxylic acid warmed with an alcohol and a little concentrated sulphuric acid gives an ester and water. The reaction is reversible and the mineral acid is only a catalyst.

\(\mathrm{R-COOH} + \mathrm{R'-OH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{R-COOR'} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

**Step 1 : protonation of the carbonyl oxygen.** The catalyst gives a proton to the doubly bonded oxygen of the acid. The cation so formed is resonance stabilised and its carbonyl carbon is a far stronger electrophile than before.

\(\mathrm{R-COOH} + \mathrm{H^{\oplus}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{R-C(OH)_2^{\oplus}}\)

**Step 2 : nucleophilic attack by the alcohol.** A lone pair on the oxygen of the alcohol attacks that carbon and a tetrahedral intermediate is obtained, in which the attacking oxygen carries the positive charge.

\(\mathrm{R-C(OH)_2^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{R'-OH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{R-C(OH)_2-\overset{\oplus}{O}(H)R'}\)

**Step 3 : proton transfer.** A proton moves from the attacking oxygen on to one of the two hydroxyl groups, turning it into \(\mathrm{-\overset{\oplus}{O}H_2}\), which is a good leaving group.

**Step 4 : loss of water.** The protonated hydroxyl leaves as water and the carbon-oxygen double bond is restored.

**Step 5 : loss of the proton.** The oxonium ion gives up \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\); the ester is set free and the catalyst is regenerated.

\(\mathrm{R-C(\overset{\oplus}{O}H)-OR'} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{R-CO-OR'} + \mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\)

The oxygen of the ester linkage comes from the alcohol and the oxygen of the water comes from the acid, which is why the alcohol is the nucleophile at step 2.

**Part 2 : dehydration of \(1^{\circ}\), \(2^{\circ}\) and \(3^{\circ}\) alcohols.**

An alcohol heated with concentrated sulphuric acid loses a molecule of water and gives an alkene. The ease of dehydration falls in the order \(3^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ}\), so the conditions needed become more severe in the same order :

| Alcohol | Conditions for dehydration |
|---|---|
| \(1^{\circ}\) : ethanol | conc. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\), \(443\ \mathrm{K}\) |
| \(2^{\circ}\) : propan-2-ol | \(85\%\) \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\), \(373\ \mathrm{K}\) |
| \(3^{\circ}\) : 2-methylpropan-2-ol | \(20\%\) \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\), \(358\ \mathrm{K}\) |

For \(2^{\circ}\) and \(3^{\circ}\) alcohols the change goes through a carbocation, in three steps.

**Step 1.** The hydroxyl oxygen is protonated to an oxonium ion, \(\mathrm{R-\overset{\oplus}{O}H_2}\). This converts the poor leaving group \(\mathrm{-OH}\) into water.

**Step 2.** Water leaves and a carbocation is formed. This is the slow, rate-determining step.

**Step 3.** A base present in the mixture, \(\mathrm{HSO_4^{\ominus}}\) or water, removes a hydrogen from the carbon adjacent to the positive centre and the alkene is formed.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{85\%\ \mathrm{H_2SO_4},\ 373\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH_2}\)

(Propan-2-ol) \(\longrightarrow\) (Propene)

Because step 2 governs the rate, the order of dehydration is the order of stability of the carbocation, and that is \(3^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ}\), the alkyl groups releasing electrons by their \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect and spreading the positive charge.

A \(1^{\circ}\) alcohol cannot give a carbocation stable enough for this route, so with it the loss of water and the loss of the hydrogen take place together in a single concerted step, and the severest conditions are required :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH} \xrightarrow[443\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{conc. } \mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

(Ethanol) \(\longrightarrow\) (Ethene)

Where two alkenes are possible the more substituted one predominates, by Saytzeff's rule : butan-2-ol gives but-2-ene as the major product and but-1-ene as the minor one.

stem: Write balanced chemical equations for the following: \(\text{ii}\). Action of zinc dust on phenol.
solution:
Phenol vapour passed over heated zinc dust is reduced to benzene. The zinc removes the oxygen of the hydroxyl group and is itself oxidised to zinc oxide.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{Zn} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{ZnO}\)

(Phenol) + (Zinc dust) \(\longrightarrow\) (Benzene) + (Zinc oxide)

The equation balances as written : six carbons, six hydrogens, one oxygen and one zinc atom on each side. The reaction is used to show that the ring present in phenol is a benzene ring, since the only product from the ring is benzene itself.

stem: Explain the mechanism of alkaline hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide with energy profile diagram. Define carbolic acid. How is carbolic acid prepared from benzene sulphonic acid?
solution:
**Part 1 : mechanism of alkaline hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide.**

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Br} + \mathrm{{}^{\ominus}OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH} + \mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\)

The substrate is a tertiary halide, so the substitution is unimolecular and takes place in two steps.

**Step 1 (slow, rate-determining).** The carbon-bromine bond breaks heterolytically. Bromine leaves with the bonding pair as bromide ion and a planar tertiary carbocation is left. The three methyl groups release electrons by their \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect and spread the positive charge, which is why a tertiary halide ionises so readily.

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Br} \xrightarrow{\text{slow}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\)

**Step 2 (fast).** The hydroxide ion attacks the carbocation. The cation is planar, so attack is possible from either face.

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{{}^{\ominus}OH} \xrightarrow{\text{fast}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH}\)

Only the halide takes part in the slow step, so the rate law is

\(\text{rate} = k\,[\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Br}]\)

and the reaction is first order : changing the concentration of the alkali does not change the rate.

**Energy profile diagram.** Potential energy is plotted on the vertical axis against the progress of the reaction on the horizontal axis. The curve starts at the level of the reactants, rises to a first maximum, which is the transition state of the ionisation, and falls into a shallow minimum, which is the carbocation together with the bromide ion. From that minimum it rises again to a second maximum, the transition state for the attack of the hydroxide ion, and then falls to the products, which lie below the reactants. The first maximum is the higher of the two; its height above the reactants is the energy of activation of the whole reaction, and that is the graphical statement that step 1 is rate-determining.

**Part 2 : carbolic acid.**

Carbolic acid is the common name of **phenol**, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}\), the compound in which a hydroxyl group is attached directly to a carbon atom of a benzene ring. The name is used because its aqueous solution is weakly acidic and turns blue litmus red.

**Part 3 : carbolic acid from benzene sulphonic acid.**

**Step 1 : neutralisation.** Benzene sulphonic acid is neutralised with sodium hydroxide to give its sodium salt.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-SO_3H} + \mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5-SO_3Na} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

**Step 2 : alkali fusion.** The sodium benzene sulphonate is fused with solid sodium hydroxide at \(573\ \mathrm{K}\). The sulphonate group is displaced by the oxygen of the alkali and sodium phenoxide is formed.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-SO_3Na} + 2\,\mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow[573\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{fuse}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Na_2SO_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

**Step 3 : acidification.** The phenoxide is treated with dilute hydrochloric acid, which sets the phenol free.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

(Benzene sulphonic acid) \(\longrightarrow\) (Sodium benzene sulphonate) \(\longrightarrow\) (Sodium phenoxide) \(\longrightarrow\) (Phenol)

stem: Write chemical reactions for the action of the following reagents on phenol: \(\text{i}\). Nitrating mixture \(\text{ii}\). Zinc dust.
solution:
**(i) Nitrating mixture.**

The nitrating mixture is concentrated nitric acid together with concentrated sulphuric acid. The hydroxyl group of phenol is strongly activating and ortho-para directing, so all three of those positions are nitrated and 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, known as picric acid, is obtained.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + 3\,\mathrm{HNO_3} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. } \mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_2(NO_2)_3-OH} + 3\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

(Phenol) \(\longrightarrow\) (2,4,6-Trinitrophenol, picric acid)

**(ii) Zinc dust.**

Phenol vapour passed over heated zinc dust is reduced to benzene; the zinc takes up the oxygen and is converted into zinc oxide.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{Zn} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{ZnO}\)

(Phenol) + (Zinc dust) \(\longrightarrow\) (Benzene) + (Zinc oxide)

Both equations balance, and the two reagents act on different parts of the molecule : the nitrating mixture substitutes on the ring and leaves the hydroxyl group in place, while zinc dust removes the hydroxyl oxygen and leaves the ring untouched.

stem: Write Dow process for preparation of Phenol. What is the action of bromine water on phenol?
solution:
**Dow process : preparation of phenol.**

Chlorobenzene is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide at \(623\ \mathrm{K}\) under a pressure of about \(300\) atmospheres. The chlorine of the ring is replaced by the oxygen of the alkali and sodium phenoxide is obtained; the phenoxide is then acidified to set the phenol free.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-Cl} + 2\,\mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow[300\ \text{atm}]{623\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

(Chlorobenzene) \(\longrightarrow\) (Sodium phenoxide) \(\longrightarrow\) (Phenol)

The severe conditions are needed because the bond between the ring carbon and chlorine has partial double bond character, the lone pair of chlorine being delocalised into the ring, and that carbon is \(sp^2\) hybridised, so an aryl halide is attacked by a nucleophile far less readily than an alkyl halide.

**Action of bromine water on phenol.**

Phenol reacts with bromine water at once, in the cold and without any catalyst. The hydroxyl group activates the ring so strongly that both ortho positions and the para position are brominated together, and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol separates.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + 3\,\mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3-OH}\downarrow + 3\,\mathrm{HBr}\)

(Phenol) \(\longrightarrow\) (2,4,6-Tribromophenol, white precipitate)

The disappearance of the colour of the bromine water together with the white precipitate is used as a test for phenol. Benzene under the same conditions gives no reaction at all, which shows how strongly the hydroxyl group activates the ring.

stem: How is methoxyethane prepared from: \(\text{i}\). Methyl iodide \(\text{ii}\). Diazomethane.
solution:
Methoxyethane is the mixed ether \(\mathrm{CH_3-O-CH_2-CH_3}\), carrying a methyl group and an ethyl group on the same oxygen.

**(i) From methyl iodide : Williamson synthesis.**

Sodium ethoxide, obtained by dissolving sodium in ethanol, supplies the alkoxide ion. The ethoxide is a strong nucleophile; it attacks the carbon of methyl iodide from the side opposite the iodine and displaces iodide in a bimolecular substitution. Methyl iodide is unhindered, so substitution takes place cleanly and elimination does not compete.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-I} + \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-O-CH_2-CH_3} + \mathrm{NaI}\)

(Methyl iodide) + (Sodium ethoxide) \(\longrightarrow\) (Methoxyethane) + (Sodium iodide)

**(ii) From diazomethane.**

Ethanol is treated with diazomethane in the presence of fluoroboric acid as catalyst. The methyl group of diazomethane replaces the hydrogen of the hydroxyl group and nitrogen gas is evolved, which drives the change to completion.

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-OH} + \mathrm{CH_2N_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HBF_4}} \mathrm{CH_3-O-CH_2-CH_3} + \mathrm{N_2}\uparrow\)

(Ethanol) + (Diazomethane) \(\longrightarrow\) (Methoxyethane) + (Nitrogen)

In both routes one methyl group and one ethyl group finish on the same oxygen, which is what the formula \(\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5}\) requires.

stem: How is diethyl ether prepared by continuous etherification process?
solution:
Diethyl ether is manufactured from ethanol and concentrated sulphuric acid at about \(413\ \mathrm{K}\). The process is called continuous because a steady stream of ethanol is run into the hot acid, and the acid used up in the first step is set free again in the second, so a small quantity of it goes on converting a large quantity of the alcohol.

**Step 1.** Ethanol reacts with concentrated sulphuric acid to give ethyl hydrogen sulphate.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5HSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

(Ethanol) + (Sulphuric acid) \(\longrightarrow\) (Ethyl hydrogen sulphate) + (Water)

**Step 2.** The ethyl hydrogen sulphate is heated at \(413\ \mathrm{K}\) with a fresh quantity of ethanol. Diethyl ether distils over and the sulphuric acid is regenerated.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5HSO_4} + \mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} \xrightarrow{413\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)

(Ethyl hydrogen sulphate) + (Ethanol) \(\longrightarrow\) (Diethyl ether) + (Sulphuric acid)

Adding the two steps gives the overall change

\(2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} \xrightarrow[413\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{conc. } \mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

in which the sulphuric acid does not appear at all. That is the check on the scheme : the acid is a catalyst, and it is precisely this that allows the ethanol to be fed in continuously. The temperature must be held near \(413\ \mathrm{K}\); if it is raised towards \(443\ \mathrm{K}\) the alcohol is dehydrated to ethene instead of giving the ether.

stem: Explain continuous etherification process for the preparation of diethyl ether.
solution:
In the continuous etherification process ethanol is converted into diethyl ether by concentrated sulphuric acid at about \(413\ \mathrm{K}\). It is called continuous because a steady stream of ethanol is fed into the hot acid, and the acid consumed in the first step is recovered in the second, so a small quantity of acid converts a large quantity of alcohol.

**Step 1 : formation of ethyl hydrogen sulphate.** Ethanol reacts with concentrated sulphuric acid.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5HSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

(Ethanol) + (Sulphuric acid) \(\longrightarrow\) (Ethyl hydrogen sulphate) + (Water)

**Step 2 : formation of the ether.** The ethyl hydrogen sulphate is heated at \(413\ \mathrm{K}\) with more ethanol. The ether distils over as it is formed and the sulphuric acid is set free to act again.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5HSO_4} + \mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} \xrightarrow{413\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)

(Ethyl hydrogen sulphate) + (Ethanol) \(\longrightarrow\) (Diethyl ether) + (Sulphuric acid)

The two steps added together give

\(2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} \xrightarrow[413\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{conc. } \mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The sulphuric acid cancels between the two steps, which shows that it acts as a catalyst and explains why the alcohol can be run in continuously. Control of the temperature is essential : near \(413\ \mathrm{K}\) the ether is obtained, while near \(443\ \mathrm{K}\) the same reagents dehydrate the alcohol to ethene.

stem: Write chemical reactions for the following reagents on methoxyethane: \(\text{(i)}\) \(hot\ \text{HI }\) \(\text{(ii)}\) \(\text{PCl}_{5}\) (iii) dilute \(\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}\).
solution:
Methoxyethane is \(\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5}\), an ether carrying two different primary alkyl groups.

**(i) Hot HI.**

Hydrogen iodide first protonates the ethereal oxygen, which turns one alkyl group into a good leaving group as an alcohol. The iodide ion then attacks by a bimolecular substitution at the less hindered of the two carbons, and that is the methyl carbon. Methyl iodide is therefore formed and the larger group is left as the alcohol.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-I} + \mathrm{C_2H_5-OH}\)

(Methoxyethane) \(\longrightarrow\) (Iodomethane) + (Ethanol)

When hot hydrogen iodide is present in excess the ethanol produced is itself converted into the iodide, so both fragments finally appear as alkyl iodides.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} + \mathrm{HI} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_2H_5-I} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

**(ii) \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\).**

Phosphorus pentachloride cleaves the ether at both carbon-oxygen bonds. Each alkyl group is obtained as its chloride and the oxygen is carried away in phosphoryl chloride, so no alcohol is left behind.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{PCl_5} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-Cl} + \mathrm{C_2H_5-Cl} + \mathrm{POCl_3}\)

(Methoxyethane) \(\longrightarrow\) (Methyl chloride) + (Ethyl chloride) + (Phosphoryl chloride)

**(iii) Dilute \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\).**

Ethers are hydrolysed by hot dilute sulphuric acid under pressure, and the two alcohols corresponding to the two alkyl groups are obtained.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow[\Delta,\ \text{pressure}]{\text{dil. } \mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3-OH} + \mathrm{C_2H_5-OH}\)

(Methoxyethane) \(\longrightarrow\) (Methanol) + (Ethanol)

Cold concentrated sulphuric acid brings about no such hydrolysis; it merely protonates the ethereal oxygen and the ether dissolves in it as an oxonium salt.

stem: What are ethers? How are they classified?
solution:
**Ethers** are the class of organic compounds in which two alkyl or aryl groups are joined to the same oxygen atom. They may be looked upon as derivatives of water in which both the hydrogen atoms have been replaced by hydrocarbon groups, or as the anhydrides of alcohols. The general formula is

\(\mathrm{R-O-R'}\)

where \(\mathrm{R}\) and \(\mathrm{R'}\) are alkyl or aryl groups. The two bonds at oxygen make an angle of about \(110^{\circ}\), so the molecule is bent and slightly polar; but there is no hydrogen on the oxygen, so one ether molecule cannot hydrogen bond to another.

**Classification.** Ethers are classified in two ways.

**1. According to whether the two groups are alike.**

- **Simple or symmetrical ethers**, in which both groups are the same, \(\mathrm{R-O-R}\). Examples : dimethyl ether \(\mathrm{CH_3-O-CH_3}\), diethyl ether \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5}\).

- **Mixed or unsymmetrical ethers**, in which the two groups are different, \(\mathrm{R-O-R'}\). Examples : methoxyethane \(\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5}\), anisole \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-O-CH_3}\).

**2. According to the nature of the groups attached to the oxygen.**

- **Dialkyl ethers**, in which both groups are alkyl, for example diethyl ether \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5}\).

- **Alkyl aryl ethers**, in which one group is alkyl and the other aryl, for example anisole \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-O-CH_3}\).

- **Diaryl ethers**, in which both groups are aryl, for example diphenyl ether \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-O-C_6H_5}\).

The two schemes are independent of each other, so anisole is at once a mixed ether and an alkyl aryl ether.

stem: Convert the following: iii. Diethyl ether into ethyl chloride.
solution:
Phosphorus pentachloride breaks both carbon-oxygen bonds of an ether and each alkyl group leaves as its chloride. Diethyl ether is symmetrical, so the two fragments are alike and two molecules of ethyl chloride are obtained from one molecule of the ether.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{PCl_5} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5-Cl} + \mathrm{POCl_3}\)

(Diethyl ether) \(\longrightarrow\) (Ethyl chloride) + (Phosphoryl chloride)

The oxygen of the ether is carried away in phosphoryl chloride, so no alcohol is left behind and the yield is two moles of ethyl chloride for every mole of the ether taken.

stem: Convert the following: iii. Anisole to phenol.
solution:
Anisole is methoxybenzene, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-O-CH_3}\), an alkyl aryl ether. Heating it with concentrated hydriodic acid cleaves the ether linkage and phenol is obtained.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-O-CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \xrightarrow{398\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{CH_3-I}\)

(Anisole) \(\longrightarrow\) (Phenol) + (Iodomethane)

Only the bond between the oxygen and the alkyl group is broken. A lone pair of the oxygen is delocalised into the benzene ring, so the bond between the oxygen and the ring carbon has partial double bond character and is both shorter and stronger; that carbon is also \(sp^2\) hybridised, and the iodide ion cannot attack it. The methyl carbon is \(sp^3\) and unhindered, so the attack takes place there, and the aryl fragment keeps the oxygen and comes away as phenol.

stem: Write preparation of (a) diethyl ether from ethyl bromide.
solution:
Diethyl ether, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5}\), is a symmetrical ether and is prepared in two standard ways.

**1. Williamson synthesis, from ethyl bromide.**

Sodium ethoxide is first made by dissolving sodium in ethanol.

\(2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{H_2}\uparrow\)

The ethoxide ion is a strong nucleophile. It attacks the carbon carrying the bromine from the side opposite the halogen and displaces bromide in a bimolecular substitution. Ethyl bromide is a primary halide, so substitution takes place cleanly and elimination does not compete.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-Br} + \mathrm{C_2H_5-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{NaBr}\)

(Ethyl bromide) + (Sodium ethoxide) \(\longrightarrow\) (Diethyl ether) + (Sodium bromide)

**2. Continuous etherification, from ethanol.**

Ethanol is run into concentrated sulphuric acid at about \(413\ \mathrm{K}\). Ethyl hydrogen sulphate is formed first, and it reacts with more ethanol to give the ether and to set the acid free again.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5HSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5HSO_4} + \mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} \xrightarrow{413\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{C_2H_5-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)

The acid cancels between the two steps and so acts only as a catalyst, which is what allows the alcohol to be fed in continuously.

stem: What is the action of phosphorous pentachloride on ethyl methyl ether?
solution:
Ethyl methyl ether is \(\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5}\). Phosphorus pentachloride cleaves both of its carbon-oxygen bonds, so each alkyl group is obtained as its chloride while the oxygen is carried away as phosphoryl chloride.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{PCl_5} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-Cl} + \mathrm{C_2H_5-Cl} + \mathrm{POCl_3}\)

(Ethyl methyl ether) \(\longrightarrow\) (Methyl chloride) + (Ethyl chloride) + (Phosphoryl chloride)

The ether is unsymmetrical, so the two chlorides obtained are different, one from each of the two alkyl groups. No alcohol is formed, because the oxygen leaves with the phosphorus; this is what distinguishes the action of \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) from the action of hot hydriodic acid, which cleaves only one of the two bonds and leaves the other group as an alcohol.

stem: Write chemical reactions for the following conversions: (i) Ethyl bromide to ethyl methyl ether.
solution:
The bromine of ethyl bromide has to be replaced by a methoxy group, so the ether is built by Williamson synthesis.

**Step 1 : preparation of the alkoxide.** Sodium is dissolved in methanol to give sodium methoxide.

\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3-OH} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CH_3-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{H_2}\uparrow\)

(Methanol) + (Sodium) \(\longrightarrow\) (Sodium methoxide) + (Hydrogen)

**Step 2 : nucleophilic substitution.** The methoxide ion attacks the carbon carrying the bromine from the side opposite the halogen and displaces bromide ion. Ethyl bromide is a primary halide, so the substitution is bimolecular and elimination does not compete with it.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-Br} + \mathrm{CH_3-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{NaBr}\)

(Ethyl bromide) + (Sodium methoxide) \(\longrightarrow\) (Ethyl methyl ether) + (Sodium bromide)

The pairing of the alkoxide with the halide matters in this synthesis. Here both fragments are primary, so the substitution succeeds; had the halide been secondary or tertiary the alkoxide would have acted as a base instead, removing a hydrogen from the carbon next to the halogen and giving an alkene in place of the ether.

stem: Why ethanol has higher boiling point than ethane?
solution:
Ethanol and ethane are of comparable size, their molecular masses being \(46\) and \(30\), yet ethanol boils at \(351\ \mathrm{K}\) \((78\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C})\) and ethane at \(184.5\ \mathrm{K}\) \((-88.6\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C})\). The difference lies in the forces acting between the molecules.

**Ethanol.** The molecule carries a hydroxyl group. Oxygen is much more electronegative than hydrogen, so the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond is strongly polar, and the hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to a lone pair on the oxygen of the next. The molecules are therefore held to one another by **intermolecular hydrogen bonds** and exist in the liquid as associated aggregates.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-O-H \cdots O(H)-C_2H_5 \cdots O(H)-C_2H_5}\)

**Ethane.** \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_3}\) is a saturated hydrocarbon. It has no polar bond and no hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom, so hydrogen bonding is impossible and the molecules are held together only by weak van der Waal's forces.

Boiling requires these intermolecular forces to be overcome. A hydrogen bond is far stronger than a van der Waal's force, so much more energy has to be supplied to separate ethanol molecules than to separate ethane molecules, and ethanol has the higher boiling point.

That molecular mass is not the deciding factor here can be seen from the two figures themselves : ethanol is the heavier molecule by only \(16\) units, yet it boils some \(166\ \mathrm{K}\) higher, a gap far too large to be accounted for by size alone.

stem: Explain, why are boiling points of carboxylic acids higher than corresponding alcohols?
solution:
Both classes of compound are associated liquids, but a carboxylic acid associates more strongly than an alcohol, and that is why it boils higher.

**An alcohol** has one oxygen and one \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond. Each molecule can donate one hydrogen and accept one hydrogen bond, so the molecules associate into open chains.

\(\mathrm{R-O-H \cdots O(H)-R \cdots O(H)-R}\)

**A carboxylic acid** has two oxygen atoms in the carboxyl group, the doubly bonded oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen. Each molecule can therefore act twice over, its \(\mathrm{O-H}\) donating a hydrogen bond while its \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) accepts one. Two molecules lock together head to tail through **two** hydrogen bonds and form a cyclic **dimer** :

\(\mathrm{R-C(=O)-O-H \cdots O{=}C(R)-O-H}\), the two molecules closing a ring through a pair of hydrogen bonds

In the liquid the acid exists largely as this dimer, whose effective molecular mass is twice that of a single molecule, and both hydrogen bonds of the dimer must be broken before a molecule can escape into the vapour. More energy is needed to do that than to break the single hydrogen bond that holds an alcohol chain together, so the boiling point of a carboxylic acid is higher than that of the corresponding alcohol.

The comparison can be made at constant molecular mass, which removes size from the argument : ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol both have molecular mass \(60\), and ethanoic acid boils at \(391\ \mathrm{K}\) against \(370\ \mathrm{K}\) for propan-1-ol.

stem: Isopropylbenzene on air oxidation followed by decomposition by dilute acid gives _____.
solution:
**(A)** \(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}\)

Isopropylbenzene is **cumene**, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH(CH_3)_2}\), and the two operations named in the question are the two steps of the cumene process, the commercial route to phenol.

**Step 1 : air oxidation.** Cumene is oxidised by atmospheric oxygen at \(423\ \mathrm{K}\) in the presence of cobalt naphthenate. The oxygen attacks the tertiary carbon-hydrogen bond of the isopropyl group, which is the weakest in the molecule, and cumene hydroperoxide is formed.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH(CH_3)_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow[423\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{Co-naphthenate}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-C(CH_3)_2-O-O-H}\)

(Cumene) + (Air) \(\longrightarrow\) (Cumene hydroperoxide)

**Step 2 : decomposition by dilute acid.** The hydroperoxide is warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid. The oxygen-oxygen bond is broken, the phenyl group migrates to the oxygen, and phenol is obtained with acetone as a by-product.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-C(CH_3)_2-O-O-H} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\)

(Cumene hydroperoxide) \(\longrightarrow\) (Phenol) + (Acetone)

The product is therefore phenol. The nine carbons of cumene are accounted for as six in phenol and three in acetone, which is the check on the scheme.

Benzoic acid and benzaldehyde arise instead from the oxidation of toluene, whose side chain carries hydrogen atoms on the benzylic carbon; and methyl benzoate would require a carboxylic acid together with methanol. None of these can come from a hydroperoxide whose oxygen ends up attached to the ring carbon.

stem: Convert the following: \(\text{ii}\). Cumene to phenol.
solution:
Cumene is isopropylbenzene, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH(CH_3)_2}\), and it is converted into phenol in two steps. This is the commercial method of manufacturing phenol.

**Step 1 : air oxidation.** Cumene is oxidised by atmospheric oxygen at \(423\ \mathrm{K}\) in the presence of cobalt naphthenate. The oxygen attacks the tertiary carbon-hydrogen bond of the isopropyl group and cumene hydroperoxide is formed.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH(CH_3)_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow[423\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{Co-naphthenate}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-C(CH_3)_2-O-O-H}\)

(Cumene) + (Air) \(\longrightarrow\) (Cumene hydroperoxide)

**Step 2 : acid decomposition.** The hydroperoxide is warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid. The oxygen-oxygen bond breaks and the products are phenol and acetone.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-C(CH_3)_2-O-O-H} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\)

(Cumene hydroperoxide) \(\longrightarrow\) (Phenol) + (Acetone)

The carbon count is consistent : the nine carbons of cumene appear as six in the phenol and three in the acetone, and the acetone is recovered as a valuable by-product, which is what makes this route economical.
